cases.name: ladder-brief
cases.promptMarkdown:
I have an idea for a feature. The pitch is in docs/pitch.md. Take it
through the idea stage as a feature run with the slug slot-finder.

Answers to the questions you would ask me, so do not stop to ask them:
the problem is that shift managers spend an evening each week rebuilding
the rota by hand after call-outs; the people who have it are
shift managers at small restaurants, who cope with a spreadsheet and a
group chat; why now is that call-outs have gone up since the schedule
moved to a phone app; the evidence is anecdote, three managers complained
in the last month. For the ambition ladder, my pick is Showstopper. The
demo I would show first is a manager tapping one call-out and the rota
filling the gap before they put the phone down. The product already knows
who is free and who is certified for each station. The riskiest piece is
ranking the replacements; a two-day spike on last month's call-outs would
prove it. The cheapest kill test is to hand-fill ten real call-outs and
see whether the ranking agrees with the manager. Success is one sentence:
a call-out is covered with no more than one tap. Do not design the
solution.

Write the brief to docs/features/slot-finder/idea.md, append any seeds to
docs/backlog.md, then print the whole brief in your reply.

# Idea: Slot finder

## Problem

Shift managers spend an evening each week rebuilding the rota by hand after
call-outs — hunting for who's free, checking who's certified for the
station, messaging around, then rewriting the schedule.

## Who has it

Shift managers at small restaurants. Today they cope with a spreadsheet and
a group chat: the call-out lands in the chat, and the manager manually
cross-references who's free against who's certified for the station, then
edits the spreadsheet by hand.

## Why now

Call-outs have gone up since the schedule moved to a phone app — easier to
flake on a shift when the ask is a tap in an app rather than a phone call to
a manager.

## Evidence

Anecdote: three managers complained about this in the last month.

## Ambition rung

Chosen: Showstopper, in the user's words: "shift managers spend an evening
each week rebuilding the rota by hand after call-outs"
Not taken: Moonshot: predict likely call-outs before they happen and
pre-arrange standby coverage — not achievable at this run's scale.
Demo: pass — before: a call-out lands in the group chat and the manager
spends an evening finding, messaging, and manually rewriting the rota;
after: the manager taps the call-out and sees the rota slot already filled
with a certified, available replacement.
Removes a step: pass — the manual search-and-fill step (checking who's free,
checking who's certified, messaging around, editing the spreadsheet) is gone
entirely, not sped up.
Only this product: pass — built on data only this product holds: who's free
and who's certified for each station.
Achievable: pass — riskiest piece is ranking the replacements; a two-day
spike against last month's call-outs could prove it.

## The demo

Before: a call-out lands in the group chat and the manager spends an evening
finding, messaging, and manually rewriting the rota. After: the manager taps
the call-out and sees the rota slot already filled with a certified,
available replacement.

## Riskiest piece + spike

Ranking the replacements — deciding who to offer the open slot to first
among everyone who is free and certified. A two-day spike running the
ranking against last month's real call-outs would show whether it picks who
a manager would have picked.

## Cheapest kill test

Hand-fill ten real call-outs and see whether the ranking agrees with the
manager's own choice.

## Solution hunch

The product already knows who is free and who is certified for each
station; a call-out should use that to fill the gap directly rather than
making the manager assemble the answer by hand. (Hunch only — no design
here.)

## Success in one sentence

A call-out is covered with no more than one tap.

## Unknowns & risks

- Whether the ranking actually agrees with what managers would pick
  themselves — the riskiest piece, unproven until the spike runs.
- Evidence is anecdotal (three managers in one month); may not generalize
  beyond small restaurants.
- "Free" and "certified" data may be stale or incomplete, which would make
  the ranking wrong before it even runs.
- Auto-filling a slot without the replacement's real-time confirmation risks
  double-booking someone who is nominally free but actually unavailable.
```

# Idea: Slot finder

## Problem

A shift manager spends an evening every week rebuilding the rota by hand
after call-outs.

## Who has it

Shift managers at small restaurants. Today they cope with a spreadsheet
and a group chat — texting around to find out who can cover, then
manually redoing the shared rota once someone answers.

## Why now

Call-outs have gone up since the schedule moved to a phone app.

## Evidence

Anecdote — three managers complained about this in the last month.

## Ambition rung

Chosen: Showstopper, in the user's words: "a manager taps one call-out and
the rota fills the gap before they put the phone down"
Not taken: Solid: surface ranked cover suggestions the manager picks from
instead of rebuilding by hand; Moonshot: predict likely call-outs and
pre-arrange standby coverage before they happen.
Demo: pass — before: manager sees the call-out and opens a spreadsheet to
start texting around; after: the rota already shows who is filling the gap.
Removes a step: pass — the evening of manual rebuilding and group-chat
texting disappears into one tap.
Only this product: pass — built on who is free and who is certified for
each station, data only this product holds.
Achievable: pass — riskiest piece is ranking replacements; a two-day spike
on last month's call-outs would prove it.

## The demo

Before: a manager gets a call-out and opens a spreadsheet to start texting
around for coverage. After: the manager taps the call-out in the app and
the rota already shows who is filling the gap.

## Riskiest piece + spike

Ranking which of the available, certified people should fill the gap. A
two-day spike replaying last month's real call-outs through a candidate
ranking would show whether the top pick matches what a manager would have
chosen.

## Cheapest kill test

Hand-fill ten real call-outs and see whether the ranking agrees with the
manager's own pick.

## Solution hunch

Use the existing free/certified-for-station data to surface and rank cover
candidates the moment a call-out is logged.

## Success in one sentence

A call-out is covered with no more than one tap.

## Unknowns & risks

- Whether the ranking actually matches what an experienced manager would
  pick — the core risk the spike targets.
- Evidence is anecdotal — three managers, no data yet on how common or
  costly call-outs are across the broader base.
- Repeatedly top-ranking the same available, certified person could burn
  them out or breed resentment among staff.
- The pitch's "self-healing rota" framing is broader than this Showstopper;
  scope must stay at the single call-out moment, not the whole week.
```
